content:
According to reports yesterday, Apple has agreed to comply with the EU's "fairer" app tracking transparency rules, following an investigation by the German antitrust watchdog.

Apple said the compliance is voluntary, and as far as we understand, it will make a total of eight changes to achieve compliance...

Developers often collect far more personal data than is necessary for the app's functionality. What Apple refers to as app tracking is one example: based on the interests shown by the apps you have installed, you are served personalised ads, which appear both in apps and on the web. App Tracking Transparency (ATT) lets users choose whether this data can be collected and used in this way.

Apple said yesterday that the Federal Cartel Office (FCO) recognises the value of giving users a choice; indeed, the FCO's report noted that it welcomes ATT from a data protection perspective, and other German privacy regulators share the same position.

The FCO's objection appears to be that Apple's existing prompt makes app tracking sound more alarming than it actually is. The iPhone maker will make eight changes to address this — including removing the word "track".

  • Change the colour of the icon element at the top of the prompt from orange to blue
  • Update the ATT prompt to display as a full page
  • Remove the word "track" from the ATT prompt and the personalised ads prompt
  • Change the ATT choice buttons from "Allow" and "Ask App Not to Track" to "Allow" and "Decline"
  • Allow formatting changes (such as bold, italics and bulleted lists) to be used in the ATT prompt
  • Add an option for developers to display an additional page of information directly from the prompt, to provide more GDPR-related information. Developers can actually already do this with a prompt shown before the ATT prompt.
  • Allow developers to re-prompt users with the ATT prompt one year after they make a decision, regardless of whether their previous choice was "agree" or "decline"
  • Make minor wording adjustments to the personalised ads prompt to make it clearer, but with no change in the effect or meaning of the wording

Apple told us it is committed to ensuring ATT continues to be available in EU countries, and said the measure is welcomed by privacy advocates, data protection authorities and iPhone users.

The company reiterated that its own apps do not display the ATT prompt, because it does not use personal data collected from apps to serve targeted advertising or measure advertising effectiveness. It stressed that it handles third-party apps in exactly the same way — if a third-party app does not collect such data, it does not need to display a prompt.

9to5Mac Opinion

This outcome appears to be the best for all parties. iPhone users will continue to make a choice, but based on a prompt that more accurately reflects the decision they are being asked to make — choosing between personalised ads and no personalised ads.

This investigation also addressed concerns about Apple's own advertising sales business. The company has clearly stated that it does not use data collected from its own apps to serve personalised ads or measure ad effectiveness.
